Run MC simulations:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Visualize the results:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Transcript

And here is the surprise, if you predicted bias. Both densities are still centered on the blue line. Omitting a variable that genuinely affects y did not bias anything, because it was uncorrelated with x-one. But look at the widths, and note that the ranking has reversed from case two. Now it is the model that omits x-two which is wider. Including a relevant variable bought you precision. So the two cases point in opposite directions, and that is not a contradiction; it is two different terms of the same formula moving.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.



EE_1EE_2




Transcript

Why is omitting a genuinely relevant variable still unbiased? The composite error v is beta-two times x-two plus u, and now beta-two is not zero, so x-two really is sitting in the error term. But the condition we need is that v is uncorrelated with x-one, and x-two is uncorrelated with x-one by construction. So the error term is inflated but not tilted. That distinction is the whole of case three: a variable in your error term is only dangerous if it is correlated with your regressor. Otherwise it is just noise.



True model
y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i

cor(x_1,x_2) = 0
\beta_2 \ne 0
E[u_i|x_{1,i},x_{2,i}]=0


Estimated model
EE_1: y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + v_{i} \;\; (v_i = \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_{i})




Question
E[v_i|x_{1,i}]=0?



Answer

Yes, because x_1 is not correlated with either x_2 or u.
So, no bias.





Transcript

The model that includes x-two is unbiased, for the same reason as always: it is the true model and the zero conditional mean condition was assumed. Nothing new here. But there is something worth noticing across the three cases so far. This estimating equation has been unbiased in every single one, because it always estimates the model that generated the data. All the interesting variation has been on the other side, in what happens when you leave something out. Case four is the first time that stops being enough.



True model
y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i

cor(x_1,x_2) = 0
\beta_2 \ne 0
E[u_i|x_{1,i},x_{2,i}]=0


Estimated model
EE_2: y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_{i}




Question
E[u_i|x_{1,i},x_{2,i}]=0?



Answer

Yes, because x_1 and x_2 are not correlated with u (by assumption). So, no bias.








EE_1EE_2EE_1 v.s. EE_2




Transcript

Now the variance, and this is the tab where case three finally differs from the earlier ones. R-squared-j is still zero, since there are no other regressors. But look at the error variance. V is beta-two times x-two plus u, and beta-two is no longer zero, so the algebra in the answer does not collapse. You get beta-two squared times the variance of x-two, plus sigma-u squared. The error variance has genuinely grown. That is the price of leaving a relevant variable in the error term.



True model
y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i

cor(x_1,x_2) = 0
\beta_2 \ne 0
E[u_i|x_{1,i},x_{2,i}]=0


Variance
Var(\widehat{\beta}_j)= \frac{\sigma_v^2}{SST_j(1-R^2_j)}
where R^2_j is the R^2 when you regress x_j on all the other covariates.

The estimated model
EE_1: y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + v_{i} \;\; (\beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_{i})





Question (R_j^2)Question (variance of the error term)


R_j^2?



Answer

0 because there are no other variables included in the model.



Var(v_i) = Var(\beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i)?



Answer

\begin{align*}
Var(error) & = Var(v_i) \\
  & = Var(\beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i) \\
  & = \beta_2^2\cdot Var(x_{2,i}) + \sigma_u^2
\end{align*}









Transcript

And for the model that includes x-two, both terms are back near their smallest values. The population relationship between x-one and x-two is zero, so sample R-squared-j is near zero rather than exactly zero. The error variance is just sigma-u squared, because x-two is properly accounted for rather than dumped into the error. The large reduction in the numerator drives the comparison in this design; the small finite-sample denominator and degrees-of-freedom differences do not overturn it.



True model
y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i

cor(x_1,x_2) = 0
\beta_2 \ne 0
E[u_i|x_{1,i},x_{2,i}]=0


Variance
Var(\widehat{\beta}_j)= \frac{\sigma_u^2}{SST_j(1-R^2_j)}
where R^2_j is the R^2 when you regress x_j on all the other covariates.

The estimated model
EE_2: y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_{i}





Question (R_j^2)Question (variance of the error term)


R_j^2?



Answer

R_j^2 is (on average) zero because x_1 and x_2 are not correlated. If you regress x_1 on x_2, then its R^2 is zero (on average).

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.



Var(u_i)?



Answer


Var(error) = Var(u_i) = \sigma_u^2










Transcript

The comparison now runs the other way. At the population level the regressors are orthogonal, so the multicollinearity denominator is unchanged. But the error variances differ: the model omitting x-two carries beta-two squared times the variance of x-two on top of sigma-u squared, while the model including it carries only sigma-u squared. In this design that precision gain easily dominates the small finite-sample cost of estimating another coefficient. Compare this against case two, where strong collinearity made inclusion costly.





Question


Var(\widehat{\beta}_1) in EE_1 \gtreqqless Var(\widehat{\beta}_1) in EE_2?







EE_1

R_j^2 = 0
Var(error) = Var(v_i) = \beta_2^2\cdot Var(x_{2,i}) + \sigma_u^2


EE_2

R_j^2 = 0
Var(error) = Var(u_i) = \sigma_u^2


Variance formula
Var(\widehat{\beta}_j)= \frac{Var(error)}{SST_j(1-R^2_j)}


 


Answer

So, Var(\widehat{\beta}_1) in EE_1 > Var(\widehat{\beta}_1) in EE_2









Transcript

Case three summarised, and note that both statements favour including x-two. Including a relevant but uncorrelated variable reduces your variance, because it takes explanatory power out of the error term. And omitting it leaves you unbiased, so nothing catastrophic happens if you cannot get it. That last point is genuinely useful in practice: if you can argue a missing variable is uncorrelated with your treatment, you can argue it costs you precision but not credibility. That argument is the backbone of a randomised experiment.


If you include a variable that has some explanatory power beyond x_1, but is not correlated with x_1 (EE_2), then the variance of the OLS estimator on x_1 is smaller compared to when you do not include x_2 (EE_1)
If you omit a variable that has some explanatory power beyond x_1 (EE_1), but is not correlated with x_1, then the OLS estimator on x_1 is still unbiased

title: 04: Omitted Variable Bias and Multicollinearity
text:
Case 4

SetupQuestionMC SimulationMC ResultsPredicted biasInsights: BiasInsights: VarianceSummary




Transcript

Case four, both switches flipped. X-two matters for y, and it is correlated with x-one. Read the example and the note under it. Better soil raises yield, and farmers do not apply the same nitrogen rate on good ground as on poor ground, so soil quality is related to the nitrogen decision. Now read the second bullet, which is the honest one. This is the case that actually happens. Case one is a curiosity, cases two and three are instructive, and case four is what you will face on essentially every project with observational data.

True Model
y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i

cor(x_1,x_2) \ne 0
\beta_2 \ne 0
E[u_i|x_{1,i},x_{2,i}]=0





Example


\text{corn yield} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times N + \beta_2 \times \text{soil quality} + u

better soil raises yield (\beta_2 \ne 0), and farmers apply nitrogen differently on good and poor ground (cor(x_1,x_2) \ne 0)
this is the case that actually happens in practice, and the one you have to worry about









Transcript

Three questions once more, and by now you have the tools to predict all three. Case two taught you that correlation alone does not bias anything. Case three taught you that relevance alone does not bias anything either. So what happens when both are present at once? Commit to an answer. And a fourth question I want you to hold in mind while you predict: if there is bias, can you say anything about its size and direction, or is it simply unknown? That question is where the second half of the lecture goes.

We will estimate the following models:

EE_1: y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + v_i \text{ , where } (v_i = \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i)
EE_2: y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i
(Only x_1 is included in EE_1, while x_1 and x_2 are included in EE_2)





Question


What do you think is gonna happen? Any guess?

E[\widehat{\beta}_1]=\beta_1 in EE_1? (bias?)
E[\widehat{\beta}_1]=\beta_1 in EE_2? (bias?)
Var(\widehat{\beta}_1) in EE_1 \gtreqqless Var(\widehat{\beta}_1) in EE_2?









Transcript

Read the loop and notice that it combines the two changes we made separately before. X-one and x-two share the common term mu, as in case two, so they are correlated. And the coefficient on x-two in the line that builds y is one rather than zero, as in case three, so x-two matters. Both conditions hold at once for the first time. Everything else, sample size, iterations, both regressions, is identical to the three previous cases, so any difference in the output is attributable to those two lines together.

Set up simulations:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Run MC simulations:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Visualize the results:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Transcript

And there it is. The two densities are no longer on top of each other, and one of them is nowhere near the blue line. The model that omits x-two has moved bodily to the right, centered near the red dashed line at about two, when the truth is one. It is not less precise; it is answering a different question. That is bias, and it is the first time we have seen it in this lecture. The model including x-two remains centered on the truth, exactly as it has in all four cases.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

the  blue  line is the true \beta_1 = 1; the  red dashed  line is where EE_1 is predicted to land, and we work out that number on the Predicted bias tab





Transcript

And the bias is not merely present, it is predictable to three digits. Work through the two numbers. The covariance of x-one and x-two is zero point eight one, because they share nine tenths of a common term whose variance is one. And the variance of x-one is zero point eight two. Their ratio is delta-one, about zero point nine eight eight. Multiply by beta-two, which is one, and add to the true beta-one. You get one point nine eight eight. Run the cell and compare against your own simulation. It matches.

This is the one case with bias, and it is  exactly  predictable. From the data generating process:

Cov(x_1, x_2) = Var(\mu) \times 0.9^2 = 0.81 and Var(x_1) = 0.1^2 + 0.9^2 = 0.82
so \delta_1 = \frac{Cov(x_1,x_2)}{Var(x_1)} = \frac{0.81}{0.82} \approx 0.988
and therefore E[\tilde{\beta}_1] = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \cdot \delta_1 = 1 + 1 \times 0.988 = \mathbf{1.988}

Check it against your own simulation:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Note


We have not derived that formula yet — it is on the Omitted Variable Bias (Theory) slide, two slides from here. Notice that the simulation confirmed it before we proved it, which is exactly the use of Monte Carlo simulation we described in lecture 03.







EE_1EE_2




Transcript

Now the explanation. The composite error v contains beta-two times x-two plus u. In case two, beta-two was zero so that term vanished. In case three, x-two was uncorrelated with x-one so the term was harmless. Here neither escape is available. X-two is in the error term with a non-zero coefficient, and it is correlated with x-one. So the error term is correlated with the regressor, the zero conditional mean condition fails, and beta-one-hat is biased. Both conditions were necessary, and both are now present.



True model
y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i

cor(x_1,x_2) \ne 0
\beta_2 \ne 0
E[u_i|x_{1,i},x_{2,i}]=0


Estimated model
EE_1: y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + v_{i} \;\; (v_i = \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_{i})




Question
E[v_i|x_{1,i}]=0?



Answer

No, because x_1 is correlated with x_2 and \beta_2 \ne 0.
So, there will be bias.





Transcript

The model that includes x-two is still unbiased, and this is the point of the whole lecture in one tab. Bias came not from the world being complicated, but from us leaving something out. Put x-two back in and the problem disappears entirely. That is why economists reach for controls. The catch, which the variance tabs cover next, is that x-two is highly correlated with x-one here, so including it is not free. This is the only case where you actually have to weigh one thing against the other.



True model
y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i

cor(x_1,x_2) \ne 0
\beta_2 \ne 0
E[u_i|x_{1,i},x_{2,i}]=0


Estimated model
EE_2: y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_{i}




Question
E[u_i|x_{1,i},x_{2,i}]=0?



Answer

Yes, because x_1 and x_2 are not correlated with u (by assumption). So, no bias.








EE_1EE_2EE_1 v.s. EE_2Why EE_1 won hereWhen EE_2 wins instead




Transcript

The variance terms for the model that omits x-two, and both moving parts are now active. R-squared-j is zero, as always in a one-regressor model. But the error variance has grown, exactly as in case three: beta-two squared times the variance of x-two, plus sigma-u squared. With the numbers here that is about one point eight two rather than one. So the numerator is inflated. Remember though that this estimator is also biased, so a small variance would be no comfort. Precision around the wrong number is worse than useless.



True model
y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i

cor(x_1,x_2) \ne 0
\beta_2 \ne 0
E[u_i|x_{1,i},x_{2,i}]=0


Variance
Var(\widehat{\beta}_j)= \frac{\sigma_v^2}{SST_j(1-R^2_j)}
where R^2_j is the R^2 when you regress x_j on all the other covariates.

The estimated model
EE_1: y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + v_{i} \;\; (\beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_{i})





Question (R_j^2)Question (variance of the error term)


R_j^2?



Answer

0 because there are no other variables included in the model.



Var(v_i) = Var(\beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i)?



Answer

\begin{align*}
Var(error) & = Var(v_i) \\
  & = Var(\beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i) \\
  & = \beta_2^2\cdot Var(x_{2,i}) + \sigma_u^2
\end{align*}









Transcript

And for the model that includes x-two, the error variance is back down to sigma-u squared, but R-squared-j is now large, because x-one and x-two are strongly correlated. Run the cell to see it come out around zero point nine seven. So this estimating equation has the better numerator and the much worse denominator, while the other one has the reverse. For the first time the two terms of the formula point in opposite directions, and which one wins is a question of magnitudes rather than principle.



True model
y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i

cor(x_1,x_2) \ne 0
\beta_2 \ne 0
E[u_i|x_{1,i},x_{2,i}]=0


Variance
Var(\widehat{\beta}_j)= \frac{\sigma_u^2}{SST_j(1-R^2_j)}
where R^2_j is the R^2 when you regress x_j on all the other covariates.

The estimated model
EE_2: y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_{i}





Question (R_j^2)Question (variance of the error term)


R_j^2?



Answer

R_j^2 is non-zero because x_1 and x_2 are correlated. If you regress x_1 on x_2, then its R^2 is non-zero.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.



Var(u_i)?



Answer


Var(error) = Var(u_i) = \sigma_u^2










Transcript

This comparison needs more care than the first three cases. The familiar variance formula assumes the regression error satisfies the exogeneity condition. In EE1 here, the composite error contains x-two and is correlated with x-one, so we cannot obtain its sampling variance by simply inserting the unconditional variance of that composite error into the usual formula. The Monte Carlo distributions can still illustrate bias and dispersion for this particular data-generating process, but the columns below are intuition, not a valid general variance derivation for EE1.





Question


Var(\widehat{\beta}_1) in EE_1 \gtreqqless Var(\widehat{\beta}_1) in EE_2?







EE_1

R_j^2 = 0
Var(error) = Var(v_i) = \beta_2^2\cdot Var(x_{2,i}) + \sigma_u^2


EE_2

R_j^2 \ne 0
Var(error) = Var(u_i) = \sigma_u^2


Variance formula
Var(\widehat{\beta}_j) = \frac{Var(error)}{SST_j(1-R^2_j)}


 


Answer

It depends.





Transcript

Let’s put numbers on the correctly specified EE2: R-squared-j is about zero point nine seven six, so one minus it is about zero point zero two four. That strong collinearity makes the EE2 estimate imprecise. The simulation shows that the biased EE1 estimate is less dispersed in this design. Do not justify EE1’s dispersion by plugging 1.82 into the standard exogenous-error formula, however; EE1 violates the condition under which that formula was derived.

Both terms in the variance formula moved, and they moved in opposite directions. Which one wins is a matter of magnitudes:

x_1 and x_2 are highly correlated, so R_j^2 is very high for EE_2 — this  inflates  Var(\widehat{\beta}_1) in EE_2


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


but \beta_2 = 1 and Var(x_2) \approx 0.82 are both small, so folding x_2 into the error term only raises the numerator from \sigma_u^2 = 1 to about 1.82 — a mild  penalty  for EE_1


A near-doubling of the numerator is no match for a denominator shrunk by a factor of about 40. That is why Var(\widehat{\beta}_1) in EE_1 came out  lower  than in EE_2.




Transcript

Now let’s deliberately change the data-generating process and watch the simulated ranking flip. X-one and x-two share almost nothing, so including x-two creates little multicollinearity, while x-two has a large effect and substantial independent variation. Run both cells. The simulated variances reverse their earlier ranking. This demonstrates that a biased estimator can be more or less dispersed than the correctly specified estimator depending on the design; it does not restore the invalid plug-in variance calculation for EE1.

Now let’s reverse the conditions:

x_1 and x_2 are NOT highly correlated, so R_j^2 is small for EE_2
\beta_2 = 5 and Var(x_2) \approx 5, so omitting x_2 inflates the error variance enormously

Run it and compare against the picture on the MC Results tab:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

EE_1 is now the  wide  one (Var \approx 1.8 against 0.013 for EE_2): the ranking has flipped
x_1 and x_2 still share a little of \mu, so EE_1 keeps a small bias of \beta_2\cdot\delta_1 \approx 5 \times \frac{0.01}{0.82} \approx 0.06 — tiny next to a standard deviation of 1.34, which is exactly why it is invisible in the plot









Transcript

Case four in two lines. There is a genuine bias-variance trade-off when a variable both matters and is correlated with your variable of interest. And economists tend to opt for unbiasedness. That second line is a professional norm rather than a theorem, so it is worth saying why. A biased estimate with tight standard errors will confidently tell you the wrong number, and no amount of extra data fixes it. A noisy but unbiased estimate at least tells you the truth eventually, and honestly reports how uncertain it is.


There exists bias-variance trade-off when independent variables are both important (their coefficients are non-zero) and they are correlated
Economists tend to opt for unbiasedness

title: 04: Omitted Variable Bias and Multicollinearity
text:
All four cases at once


Transcript

Here is the whole lecture on one slide. Two conditions, four cells. Read across the top row: with beta-two equal to zero, x-two is irrelevant, and the only question is whether including it costs you variance, which it does when the two are correlated. Read the bottom row: x-two matters, and now omitting it either costs variance or costs you bias. Then read the two bullets. Bias appears in exactly one cell, and it needs both conditions at once. Either one on its own, as cases two and three showed, leaves you unbiased.

The question is always the same:  should x_2 be in the model?  The answer depends on only two things.









cor(x_1,x_2) = 0
cor(x_1,x_2) \ne 0




\beta_2 = 0
Case 1: both unbiased, same variance. Including x_2 costs you nothing.
Case 2: both unbiased, but including x_2  inflates  the variance. This is multicollinearity.


\beta_2 \ne 0
Case 3: both unbiased, but  omitting  x_2 inflates the variance. Include it.
Case 4: omitting x_2 gives you bias. Including it may inflate the variance. A genuine trade-off.




Two things to carry away:

 bias  appears in exactly one cell, and it needs  both  conditions: x_2 must matter  and  be correlated with x_1. Either one alone is harmless for unbiasedness.
in the three cells with no bias, including x_2 is never worse than a variance question. Case 4 is the only one where you have to choose, and economists almost always choose unbiasedness.

title: 04: Omitted Variable Bias and Multicollinearity
text:
Omitted Variable Bias (Theory)

SetupMagnitude and direction of biasExamplesHow does this help?




Transcript

Now the algebra behind what case four showed us. Notice the two different symbols: beta-one-tilde for the estimator from the model that omits x-two, beta-one-hat for the one that includes it. Then the auxiliary regression, and read the direction carefully because this is where people go wrong. You regress the omitted variable on the included one, not the reverse. Delta-one is that slope, the covariance over the variance of x-one. The boxed result says the bias is beta-two times delta-one, and case four’s number came from exactly this.

True model
y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_i

EE_1
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + v_{i} \;\; (\beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_{i})
Let \tilde{\beta}_1 denote the estimator of \beta_1 from this model

EE_2
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + u_{i}
Let \widehat{\beta}_1 and \widehat{\beta}_2 denote the estimator of \beta_1 and \beta_2

Relationship between x_1 and x_2
Regress the  omitted  variable on the  included  one:
x_{2,i} = \delta_0 + \delta_1 x_{1,i} + e_{i}, so that \delta_1 = \frac{Cov(x_1,x_2)}{Var(x_1)}




Important


Then, E[\tilde{\beta}_1] = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \cdot \delta_1, where \beta_2 \cdot \delta_1 is the bias.



That is, if you omit x_2 and regress y only on x_1, then the bias is the product of the impact of x_2 on y (\beta_2) and the slope you would get from regressing x_2 on x_1 (\delta_1).

note the  direction  of that auxiliary regression: omitted on included, not the other way around





Transcript

The four sign combinations, and they follow directly from the formula. Bias is beta-two times delta-one, and delta-one has the same sign as the correlation, so the sign of the bias is just the product of two signs. Work through the first line to convince yourself and the rest will follow. Then read the magnitude bullets and the note. The bias grows with the correlation and with the size of beta-two. It does not depend on beta-one at all. The coefficient you care about could be huge or zero; the bias is the same either way.

Direction of bias

Cor(x_1, x_2) > 0 and \beta_2 >0, then bias > 0
Cor(x_1, x_2) > 0 and \beta_2 <0, then bias < 0
Cor(x_1, x_2) < 0 and \beta_2 >0, then bias < 0
Cor(x_1, x_2) < 0 and \beta_2 <0, then bias > 0


Magnitude of bias

Holding the standard deviations of x_1 and x_2 fixed, the greater |Cor(x_1,x_2)| is, the greater the absolute bias
The greater |\beta_2| is, the greater the bias





Note


\beta_1 — the coefficient you actually care about — plays  no role  in the bias. Omitting x_2 shifts \widehat{\beta}_1 by \beta_2\cdot\delta_1 regardless of how large or small the true effect of x_1 is.







Example 1Example 2Example 3




Transcript

Work this one out yourself before I say anything. Nitrogen is your variable of interest, soil erodibility is omitted and sits in the error term. Two facts on screen. Farmers apply more nitrogen to more erodible ground to compensate for nutrient loss, so the correlation is positive. And erodibility hurts yield, so gamma is negative. Positive correlation times negative gamma gives a negative bias. So your estimate of nitrogen’s effect on yield comes out too low. You would understate the value of fertiliser, possibly badly.


\begin{aligned}
\text{corn yield} = \alpha + \beta \cdot N + (\gamma \cdot \text{soil erodability}  + \mu)
\end{aligned}


Famers tend to apply more nitrogen to the field that is more erodible to compensate for loss of nutrient due to erosion
Soil erodability affects corn yield negatively (\gamma < 0)

What is the direction of bias on \hat{\beta}?




Transcript

This is the classic housing example, and it is worth knowing because it appears in Wooldridge and in real policy debates. You want the effect of distance to an incinerator on house prices. But planners put incinerators on the edge of town, so distance to the incinerator is negatively related to distance from the city center, and distance from the center lowers prices. Negative correlation times negative gamma gives a positive bias. So you would overstate how much being near an incinerator hurts a house’s value.


\begin{aligned}
\text{house price} = \alpha + \beta \cdot \text{dist to incinerators} + (\gamma \cdot \text{dist to city center}  + \mu)
\end{aligned}


The city planner placed incinerators in the outskirt of a city to avoid their potentially negative health effects
Distance to city center has a negative impact on house price (\gamma < 0)

What is the direction of bias on \hat{\beta}?




Transcript

One from my own field. You are estimating the effect of precipitation on groundwater use, and irrigation technology is omitted. Farmers in drier places adopt center pivot more, so precipitation is negatively correlated with center pivot adoption. And center pivot applies water more efficiently, so gamma is negative. Negative times negative gives a positive bias. Now notice something useful: you would expect the true effect of precipitation on groundwater use to be negative, and the bias pushes upward, against your expectation. The next tab is about why that is good news.


\begin{aligned}
\text{groundwater use} = \alpha + \beta \cdot \text{precipitation} + (\gamma \cdot \text{center pivot}  + \mu)
\end{aligned}

\text{groundwater use}: groundwater use by a farmer for irrigated production
\text{center pivot}: 1 if center pivot is used, 0 if flood irrigation (less effective) is used

Farmers who have relatively low precipitation during the growing season tend to adopt center pivot more
center pivot applied water more efficiently than flood irrigation (\gamma < 0)

What is the direction of bias on \hat{\beta}?






When the direction of the bias is the  opposite  of the expected coefficient on the variable of interest, you can claim that  even after  suffering from the bias, you are still seeing the impact of the variable interest. So, it is strong evidence that you would have had an even stronger estimated impact.

Example 1Example 2




Transcript

Here is why signing the bias is worth the effort. The true effect is minus ten, the bias is plus five, so what you actually estimate is minus five. You never see the first two numbers, only the last. But if you can argue the bias is positive, then your estimate of minus five is a conservative one: the truth must be even more negative. So you can say, with a straight face, that the effect is at least this large. The bias worked against you and the result survived anyway.


\begin{aligned}
\text{groundwater use} = \alpha + \beta \cdot \text{precipitation} + (\gamma \cdot \text{center pivot}  + \mu)
\end{aligned}


The true \beta is -10 ( you do not observe this )
The bias on \widehat{\beta} is 5 ( you do not observe this )
\widehat{\beta} is -5 ( you only observe this )

You believe the direction of bias is positive (you need provide reasoning behind your belief), and yet, the estimated coefficient is still negative. So, you can be quite confident that the sign of the impact of precipitation is negative. You can say your estimate is a conservative estimate of the impact of precipitation on groundwater use.




Transcript

And here is the case where the same reasoning gives you nothing. True effect minus ten, bias minus five, estimate minus fifteen. Again you see only the last number. But now the bias points the same direction as your finding, so it could be doing all the work. A large enough negative bias could produce a negative estimate even if the truth were positive. Read the last sentence: there is nothing you can do. The direction of the bias determines whether this argument is available to you, and you do not get to choose it.


\begin{aligned}
\text{house price} = \alpha + \beta \cdot \text{dist to incinerators} + (\gamma \cdot \text{dist to city center}  + \mu)
\end{aligned}


The true \beta is -10 ( you do not observe this )
The bias on \widehat{\beta} is -5 ( you do not observe this )
\widehat{\beta} is -15 ( you only observe this )

You believe the direction of bias is negative, and the estimated coefficient is negative. So, unlike the case above, you cannot be confident that \widehat{\beta} would have been negative if it were not for the bias (by observing dist to city center and include it as a covariate). It is very much possible that the degree of bias is so large that the estimated coefficient turns negative even though the true sign of \beta is positive. In this case, there is nothing you can do.

title: 02: Multivariate Regression
text:
Univariate vs Multivariate Regression Models

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Bi-variate vs. Uni-variateExampleExampleModel (general)




Transcript

Let’s start with why we are doing this at all. In the univariate world the zero conditional mean condition is almost certainly violated, and the reason is structural: every variable you did not include is sitting in the error term, and any one of them can be correlated with your x. So the fix suggests itself. Move some of those variables out of the error term and into the model. Each one you include is one fewer thing that can bias you. But read the word in blue carefully. Less severe, not solved. That qualifier is the honest part of the sentence, and we come back to it.

Univariate
The most important assumption E[u|x] = 0 (zero conditional mean) is almost always violated (unless your data comes from randomized experiments) because all the other variables are sitting in the error term, which can be correlated with x.

Multivariate
More independent variables mean fewer factors left in the error term, which makes the endogeneity problem  less severe




Transcript

Here is the move written out. On top, the univariate model, where the error term u-one contains experience; look at the parenthesis, u-one equals u-two plus beta-two times experience. Underneath, the bivariate model, where experience has been pulled out and given its own coefficient. Now read the two bullets. In the first model beta-one-hat is biased unless experience happens to be uncorrelated with education, which it certainly is not. In the second you can measure the effect of education holding experience fixed. That is what the phrase in red means: we say experience has been controlled for.

Uni-variate vs. bi-variate
\begin{align*}
  \text{Uni-variate}\;\; wage = & \beta_0 + \beta_1 educ + u_1 (=u_2+\beta_2 exper)\\
  \text{Bi-variate}\;\; wage = & \beta_0 + \beta_1 educ + \beta_2 exper + u_2
\end{align*}

What’s different?

uni-variate: \widehat{\beta}_1 is biased unless experience is uncorrelated with education because experience was in error term
bi-variate: able to measure the effect of education on wage,  holding experience fixed  because experience is modeled explicitly ( We say exper is controlled for. )





Transcript

Same structure, a different question, and this one is worth carrying around because you will meet it in real policy debates. Does spending more per student raise test scores? Regress score on spending alone and average family income sits in the error term. But richer districts both spend more and have students who score higher for reasons that have nothing to do with the spending. So the naive regression credits the money with what the income did. Put average income into the model and you have controlled for it. Same shape as the wage example, same shape as the firefighters in lecture zero.

The impact of per student spending (expend) on standardized test score (avgscore) at the high school level
\begin{align*}
avgscore= & \beta_0+\beta_1 expend + u_1 (=u_2+\beta_2 avginc) \notag \\
avgscore= & \beta_0+\beta_1 expend +\beta_2 avginc + u_2 \notag
\end{align*}




Transcript

Now the general version, and I mostly want you to read the two bullets defining the betas, because six words there are doing a great deal of work. Beta-one describes how the conditional regression function changes with x-one while the included x-two is held fixed. That is what people mean by a partial effect, and the last section makes precise what the machinery is doing. Be careful, though: including x-two creates a conditional comparison; it does not automatically make that comparison causal. We still need the zero conditional mean assumption for the remaining error.

More generally,
\begin{align*}
  y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + u
\end{align*}

\beta_0: intercept
\beta_1: measure the change in y with respect to x_1, holding other factors fixed
\beta_2: measure the change in y with respect to x_2, holding other factors fixed

title: 02: Multivariate Regression
section: The Crucial Condition (Assumption) for Unbiasedness of the OLS Estimator
text:
The Crucial Condition (Assumption) for Unbiasedness of the OLS Estimator

Uni-variate v.s. Bi-variateMean independence condition: example




Transcript

The condition for unbiasedness generalises in the way you would guess. In the univariate case it was the expected value of u given x equals zero. Now it is the expected value of u given x-one and x-two equals zero. Read the verbal version, because it is a stronger statement than it looks: for any combination of values of x-one and x-two, the unobservables average to zero. Not for each variable separately, but for every pairing of them. Adding regressors moves things out of u, which helps. It also makes the condition you need slightly more demanding to state.

Uni-variate
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + u,
E[u|x]=0

Bi-variate
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + u,

Mathematically: E[u|x_1,x_2]=0
Verbally: for any values of x_1 and x_2, the expected value of the unobservables is zero





Transcript

Here it is for the wage model. The condition is that the expected value of u for every combination of education and experience is zero. If innate ability remains in u, this requires its conditional average not to vary across those combinations. Say that out loud and ask whether you believe it. More able people tend to stay in school longer, so probably not. Now read the callout, which is the honest summary of this whole lecture. Adding experience took experience out of the error term. Nothing takes ability out, because you never measured it. Regression changes the contents of the error term; it does not empty it.

In the following wage model,
\begin{align*}
wage = & \beta_0 + \beta_1 educ + \beta_2 exper + u
\end{align*}
Mean independence condition is
\begin{align*}
  E[u|educ,exper]=0
\end{align*}
Verbally:
This condition would be satisfied if innate ability of students is on average unrelated to education level and experience.




The limit of controlling for things


Notice what just happened. Adding exper to the model moved experience  out  of the error term, so it can no longer bias us. But ability is still in there, and no amount of extra regressors will move it out, because  you cannot control for something you do not observe . Multivariate regression shrinks the error term. It does not empty it.

title: 02: Multivariate Regression
section: The model with k independent variables
text:
The model with k independent variables

General modelImplementation (R)Present results(Math: derive OLS estimator)




Transcript

The extension to k variables involves no new ideas, only longer expressions. The model is y equals beta-zero plus beta-one x-one, out to beta-k x-k, plus u. And the condition for unbiasedness is that the expected value of u given the entire vector of regressors equals zero. This joint conditional statement is stronger than requiring zero pairwise correlation between u and each regressor. If it fails, the affected coefficient estimates may be biased; which coefficients are affected and by how much depends on the relationships among the regressors and the omitted component.

Model
\begin{align*}
  y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_k x_k + u
\end{align*}

Mean independence assumption?
\beta_{OLS} (OLS estimators of \betas) is unbiased if,
\begin{align*}
    E[u|x_1,x_2,\dots,x_k]=0
\end{align*}
Verbally: this condition would be satisfied if the error term is uncorrelated with any of the independent variables, x_1,x_2,\dots,x_k.




Transcript

Here it is in code, and notice how little changes. You write feols, then y tilde x-one plus x-two, and you have gone from univariate to multivariate by typing four characters. That is the entire syntactic difference. But look at what the simulation does: I built the data myself, so I know the truth. The intercept is one and both slopes are one. So when you run this you are not just reading output, you are checking it. Compare the estimates against the true values and see how close OLS gets with a hundred observations.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Note the true values: the intercept is 1, and both slopes are 1. Compare them with what OLS returns.




Transcript

On the left is the code, on the right is what it produces: a proper regression table, coefficients with standard errors underneath in parentheses, and stars for significance. The problemThe FOCsMore succinctly




Transcript

The derivation is the same story as lecture 01-2, just with more unknowns, so this should feel familiar rather than new. We are choosing the whole collection of beta-hats, which I am calling theta-hat to save writing, to minimize the sum of squared residuals. That is the identical criterion. The only change is that the thing inside the bracket now has k terms in it instead of two. If you followed the univariate version you have already followed this one, and the next tab just turns the handle.

OLS
Find the combination of \betas that minimizes the sum of squared residuals

So,
Denoting the collection of \widehat{\beta}s as \widehat{\theta} (=\{\widehat{\beta}_0,\widehat{\beta}_1,\dots,\widehat{\beta}_k\}),
\begin{align*}
    Min_{\widehat{\theta}} \sum_{i=1}^n \Big[ y_i-(\widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_1 x_{1,i} + \widehat{\beta}_2 x_{2,i} + \dots + \widehat{\beta}_k x_{k,i}) \Big]^2
\end{align*}
Exactly the univariate problem from lecture 01-2, with k+1 unknowns instead of two: an intercept and k slope coefficients.




Transcript

Turn the handle: differentiate with respect to each of the k plus one unknowns, set every derivative to zero, and divide out the minus two. What you get is k plus one equations. Look at their shape. The first is the sum of the residuals. The second is the sum of x-one times the residuals. And so on down to x-k. Every regressor gets its own equation, and every equation says the same thing, that this regressor must be uncorrelated with what is left over. Which is the sample version of the assumption we just made about the population.

Partially differentiate the objective function (sum of squared residuals) with respect to each of \widehat{\theta} (=\{\widehat{\beta}_0,\widehat{\beta}_1,\dots,\widehat{\beta}_k\}) and set each to zero. Dividing each by -2 leaves k+1 equations:
\begin{align*}
  \sum_{i=1}^n \Big[ y_i-(\widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_1 x_{1,i} + \widehat{\beta}_2 x_{2,i} + \dots + \widehat{\beta}_k x_{k,i}) \Big] = & 0 \;\; (\widehat{\beta}_0) \\
  \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i,1}\Big[ y_i-(\widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_1 x_{1,i} + \widehat{\beta}_2 x_{2,i} + \dots + \widehat{\beta}_k x_{k,i}) \Big]= & 0  \;\; (\widehat{\beta}_1) \\
  \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i,2}\Big[ y_i-(\widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_1 x_{1,i} + \widehat{\beta}_2 x_{2,i} + \dots + \widehat{\beta}_k x_{k,i}) \Big]= & 0  \;\; (\widehat{\beta}_2) \\
  \vdots \\
  \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i,k}\Big[ y_i-(\widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_1 x_{1,i} + \widehat{\beta}_2 x_{2,i} + \dots + \widehat{\beta}_k x_{k,i}) \Big]= & 0  \;\; (\widehat{\beta}_k)
\end{align*}




Transcript

And here is the compact form, which is worth committing to memory because it recurs constantly. The residuals sum to zero, and each x times the residuals sums to zero. That is k plus one equations in k plus one unknowns. The solution is unique when the regressor matrix has full column rank—the no-perfect-collinearity condition introduced shortly. Read the last line too, because it is not decoration. Estimating those k plus one coefficients uses k plus one degrees of freedom. That is where n minus k minus one comes from when we estimate sigma squared, two tabs from now.

Every bracket above is just the residual \widehat{u}_i, so the whole system is:
\begin{align*}
  \sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{u}_i = & 0 \;\; (\widehat{\beta}_0) \\
  \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i,1}\widehat{u}_i = & 0  \;\; (\widehat{\beta}_1) \\
  \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i,2}\widehat{u}_i = & 0  \;\; (\widehat{\beta}_2) \\
  \vdots \\
  \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i,k}\widehat{u}_i = & 0  \;\; (\widehat{\beta}_k)
\end{align*}
k+1 equations in k+1 unknowns. That count is what costs you k+1 degrees of freedom later.

title: 02: Multivariate Regression
text:
Unbiasedness of OLS Estimators

Conditions (four)Perfect CollinearityEndogeneity (Definition)




Transcript

Four conditions for unbiasedness, and they are the same four you met in lecture 01-3, relabelled MLR for multiple regression. Your model is correct. Your sample is random. No perfect collinearity, which is the new one, replacing the old requirement that x actually varies. And zero conditional mean, which is again the one that matters. Three of these are cheap. The fourth you will spend a career arguing about, and notice that adding regressors changes what it demands of you, because now it has to hold given all of them at once.




Important


OLS estimators of multivariate models are unbiased if the following conditions are satisfied.






Condition 1
Your model is correct (Assumption MLR.1)

Condition 2
Random sampling (Assumption MLR.2)





Condition 3
No perfect collinearity (Assumption MLR.3)

Condition 4
Zero Conditional Mean (Assumption MLR.4)
E[u|x_1,x_2,\dots,x_k]=0







Transcript

The genuinely new condition. No independent variable may be an exact linear function of the others. The example is deliberately silly: you put education in the model, and then you also put in three times education. There is no way to separate those two effects, because whenever one moves the other moves in lockstep, perfectly predictably. The data simply contains no information about which of the two is responsible. R will not throw an error either; it will quietly drop one and tell you. Where this actually bites is dummy variables, which is a later lecture.

No Perfect Collinearity (MLR.3)
Any variable cannot be a linear function of the other variables

Example (silly)
\begin{align*}
  wage = \beta_0 + \beta_1 educ + \beta_2 (3\times educ) + u
\end{align*}
( More on this later when we talk about dummy variables)




Transcript

Here is endogeneity written formally at last, though we have been circling it since lecture zero. The expected value of u given your regressors is some function of them, rather than zero. Now look at the list of what causes it. Functional form misspecification: if the truth is logarithmic and you fit a straight line, the mismatch goes into the error term, and it is a function of x by construction. Omitted variables you already know about. And more sources are coming. The point of the list is that endogeneity is a family of problems, not a single mistake.





Endogeneity: Definition



E[u|x_1,x_2,\dots,x_k] = f(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_k) \ne 0






What could cause endogeneity problem?

functional form misspecification

\begin{align*}
  wage = & \beta_0 + \beta_1 log(x_1) + \beta_2 x_2 + u_1 \;\;\text{(true)}\\
  wage = & \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + u_2 \;\; \text{(yours)},\;\; \text{where } u_2 = u_1 + \beta_1[log(x_1)-x_1]
\end{align*}

omission of variables that are correlated with any of x_1,x_2,\dots,x_k ( more on this soon )
 other sources of endogeneity later

title: 02: Multivariate Regression
02: Multivariate Regression
text:
Frisch–Waugh–Lovell Theorem


Transcript

This section is optional, but I would encourage you to follow it, because it explains what controlling for a variable actually does, mechanically. There are two ways to get the coefficient on x-one. Method one is what you already do: throw everything into a single regression. Method two takes three steps. Regress y on the other variables and keep the residuals. Regress x-one on the other variables and keep those residuals. Then regress the first set of residuals on the second. The theorem says the two routes give exactly the same number. Not approximately the same.

Consider the following simple model,
\begin{align*}
  y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + \beta_3 x_{3,i} + u_i
\end{align*}
Suppose you are interested in estimating only \beta_1.
Let’s consider the following two methods,

Method 1: Regular OLS
Regress y on x_1, x_2, and x_3 with an intercept to estimate \beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3 at the same time (just like you normally do)

Method 2: 3-step

regress y on x_2 and x_3 with an intercept and get residuals, which we call \widehat{u}_y
regress x_1 on x_2 and x_3 with an intercept and get residuals, which we call \widehat{u}_{x_1}
regress \widehat{u}_y on \widehat{u}_{x_1} (\widehat{u}_y=\alpha_1 \widehat{u}_{x_1}+v_3)

Frisch-Waugh–Lovell theorem
Methods 1 and 2 produce the same coefficient estimate on x_1
\widehat{\beta}_1 = \widehat{\alpha_1}

title: 02: Multivariate Regression
text:
Frisch–Waugh–Lovell: see it happen


Transcript

Rather than assert it, run it. The first cell simulates data where x-one is deliberately correlated with x-two and x-three, so that the partialling out has real work to do. The next two run each method in turn, and the last one prints the two coefficients side by side. Look at them. They agree to every digit shown, and the actual difference is about four times ten to the minus sixteen, which is the smallest gap the computer can represent. These are not two procedures that happen to give similar answers. It is one procedure written two different ways.

Do not take it on faith. Run both methods on the same simulated data and compare.
Step 1: generate the data. x1 is built from x2 and x3, so they really do share variation.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Step 2: Method 1. Regress y on everything at once.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Step 3: Method 2. Partial x_2 and x_3 out of both y and x_1, then regress one set of residuals on the other.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Step 4: compare.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Not merely close: identical to machine precision. The difference is about -4\times 10^{-16}, which is rounding, not disagreement.

title: 02: Multivariate Regression
text:
Partialing out Interpretation from Method 2


Transcript

Now let’s read those three steps for meaning rather than mechanics. Step one gives you the part of y that x-two and x-three cannot explain, y with their influence stripped out. Step two does the same thing to x-one, leaving the part of x-one that is unrelated to the others. Step three regresses one leftover on the other. So the coefficient on x-one is computed only from variation in x-one that the other regressors could not account for. Everything they could account for has been removed from both sides before the comparison is made.

Step 1
Regress y on x_2 and x_3 with an intercept and get residuals, which we call \widehat{u}_y

\widehat{u}_y is void of the impact of x_2 and x_3 on y

Step 2
Regress x_1 on x_2 and x_3 with an intercept and get residuals, which we call \widehat{u}_{x_1}

\widehat{u}_{x_1} is void of the impact of x_2 and x_3 on x_1

Step 3
Regress \widehat{u}_y on \widehat{u}_{x_1}, which produces an estimate of \beta_1 identical to the one you get from regressing y on x_1, x_2, and x_3

title: 02: Multivariate Regression
text:
Interpretation


Transcript

So here is what to take from the whole section. When you run a multivariate regression, the coefficient on your variable of interest comes from the variation that the other variables cannot explain. That is what controlling for something means, mechanically. Read the second bullet, which is the payoff: including a variable stops you confusing its effect with the effect you actually want. And now recall the caveat from earlier in the lecture. This works beautifully for the variables you include, and does nothing whatever for the ones you never measured.


Regressing y on all explanatory variables (x_1, x_2, and x_3) in a multivariate regression is as if you are looking at the impact of a single explanatory variable with the effects of all the other variables partialled out
In other words, including variables beyond your variable of interest lets you  control for (remove the effect of)  other variables, avoiding confusing the impact of the variable of interest with the impact of other variables.

title: 01-2: Univariate Regression: OLS Mechanics and Implementation
text:
The data set and model

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Set upR code to get dataData visualization




Transcript

Let’s start with a concrete data set, because everything from here on is done on real numbers. We have five hundred and forty-six houses, and for each one we know the sale price and the lot size. The model is on screen: price for house i equals beta-zero, plus beta-one times lot size for house i, plus u-i. Same shape as everything in the last lecture. And the objective is simple to state, estimate the impact of lot size on house price. Notice how much work u-i is doing. Bedrooms, bathrooms, the neighbourhood, the year of sale, all of it sits inside that one term.

Data
Observations of house price and lot size for 546 houses.

Model
price_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 lotsize_i+u_i

price_i: house price ($) of house i
lotsize_i: lot size of house i
u_i: error term (everything else) of house i


Objective
Estimate the impact of lot size on house price




Transcript

Here is the code that gets you the data, and this is a live R session running inside your browser, so you can edit it and press run. We load the AER package, which is where the HousePrices data lives, then call data to bring it into memory. The dataset has twelve columns, but the final line selects and previews only the two we use in this lecture: price and lot size. Do run it yourself rather than just reading it. The first time you press run it takes a moment, because R itself is downloading into the tab.



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.





Transcript

Before you estimate anything, look at your data. This is house price up the vertical axis against lot size along the horizontal. Two things to notice. First, there is clearly a positive relationship; bigger lots do sell for more. Second, and more important, look at the vertical spread at any given lot size. Take lot size four thousand and run your eye upwards: prices there range from about thirty thousand to well over a hundred thousand. That spread is the error term, made visible. Our job is to put one line through this cloud, and the scatter tells you in advance that no line will fit it well.



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 01-2: Univariate Regression: OLS Mechanics and Implementation
text:
Estimation with OLS

Rough ideaExamplesResidualsOLSVisualizationDerivationEstimators vs Estimates




Transcript

So here is the goal as a picture. We want to draw a line like this one through the cloud, and the slope of that line is our estimate of beta-one. The method is called ordinary least squares, OLS, and you will use it for the rest of your career. But notice I have quietly done something unjustified: I drew a line. Why this line, and not one slightly steeper, or shifted up a little? There are infinitely many lines available and I have not told you how to choose between them. The next few tabs are about answering that honestly.


We want to draw a line like this, the slope of which is an estimate of \beta_1
A way: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.




Ex. 1: \widehat{\beta}_0=20000, \widehat{\beta}_1=7Ex. 2: \widehat{\beta}_0=70000, \widehat{\beta}_1=3.8So,




Transcript

Let’s take that question seriously by trying some lines out. Here is a candidate: an intercept of twenty thousand and a slope of seven. So this line claims a house with no lot at all is worth twenty thousand, and each extra unit of lot size adds seven dollars. Look at how it sits in the cloud. It is not absurd. It runs roughly through the middle of the data, and if you had to defend it in a seminar you probably could. Hold that impression, because the next tab shows a different line that also looks defensible, and they cannot both be best.



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.





Transcript

And here is the rival: intercept seventy thousand, slope three point eight. Higher starting point, flatter line. Flip back and forth between this tab and the previous one and you will see the problem. Both lines pass through the data. Neither is obviously wrong by eye. But they say completely different things about the world. One says an extra unit of lot size is worth seven dollars, the other says under four. If you were advising somebody on whether to buy more land, that gap matters enormously. Eyeballing is not going to settle it.



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.





Transcript

Which brings us to the two questions in the box, and I want you to see that the second one is the real question. Asking which values of beta-hat-zero and beta-hat-one are best is meaningless until you say what best means. That is a decision we make, not something the data hands us. What we need is a criterion: a single number that scores any candidate line, so that comparing two lines becomes comparing two numbers. Once we have that, the whole thing turns into a minimization problem and the mathematics takes over. Defining that criterion is what the next tabs do.





Question



Among all the possible values of \widehat{\beta}_0 and \widehat{\beta}_1, which one is the best?
What criteria do we use (what does the best even mean?)













Transcript

Here is the raw material for that criterion. Pick any values of beta-hat-zero and beta-hat-one, and that gives you a modeled value for every house: beta-hat-zero plus beta-hat-one times x-i. The residual is what is left over, the actual price minus the modeled price. Look at the figure, where I have taken twenty-five houses and drawn their residuals in red. Each red segment runs from a point to the line, so a long one means the line missed that house badly. Two things to keep straight. Residuals are computable, unlike the error term u, which you never see. And move the line, and every red segment changes.

For particular values of \widehat{\beta}_0 and \widehat{\beta}_1 you pick, the modeled value of y for individual i is \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i.
Then, the residual for individual i is:

\widehat{u}_i =  y_i - (\widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i)

That is, the residual is the observed value of the dependent variable less the modeled value. For different values of \widehat{\beta}_0 and \widehat{\beta}_1, you have a different value of residual.
The vertical red segments below  are  the residuals: each one runs from an observed point to the line.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.





Transcript

Now we can state the criterion, and it is the obvious one once you have seen those red segments: choose the line that makes them small overall. Specifically, square each residual, add them all up, and pick the beta-hats that make that sum as small as it can be. That is what ordinary least squares means, and the name is a literal description: least, squares. The mathematics below says exactly the same thing in symbols, minimize over beta-hat-zero and beta-hat-one the sum from i equals one to n of u-hat-i squared. That is the whole idea. Everything that follows is just carrying out the minimization.

Idea of OLS (Ordinary Least Squares)
Let’s find the values of \widehat{\beta}_0 and \widehat{\beta}_1 that minimize the sum of the squared residuals!

Mathematically
Solve the following minimization problem:
Min_{\widehat{\beta}_0,\widehat{\beta}_1} \sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{u}_i^2, \text{where} \;\; \widehat{u}_i=y_i-(\widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_1 x_i)




Transcript

Two questions on this slide, and I want you to think about them rather than take the squaring on faith. First, why square? Suppose you just added the raw residuals up. Points above the line contribute positive numbers, points below contribute negative ones, and they cancel, so a wildly wrong line could score zero. Squaring removes the sign, and it also punishes one enormous miss more than several small ones. Second, why not absolute values? You could, and that method exists; it is called least absolute deviations. Squares win mainly because they give you something you can differentiate and solve by hand, which is exactly what we do next.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Questions

Why do we square the residuals, and then sum them up together? What’s gonna happen if you just sum up residuals?
How about taking the absolute value of residuals, and then sum them up?





Transcript

Here is the calculus, and you should watch it once even if you never do it again. We are minimizing S, the sum of squared residuals, over two unknowns, so we take a partial derivative with respect to each and set both to zero. Now look at what the two first-order conditions say once you divide out the minus two. The sum of the residuals is zero, and the sum of x times the residuals is zero. Those are not assumptions we are making; they are consequences of the arithmetic, and they hold in every OLS regression you will ever run. Solve the pair and you get the formulas at the bottom.

Minimization problem to solve
Min_{\widehat{\beta}_0,\widehat{\beta}_1} \sum_{i=1}^n [y_i-(\widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_1 x_i)]^2
Steps

partial differentiation of the objective function with respect to \widehat{\beta}_0 and \widehat{\beta}_1
solve for \widehat{\beta}_0 and \widehat{\beta}_1

Min_{\widehat{\beta}_0,\widehat{\beta}_1} \sum_{i=1}^n [y_i-(\widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_1 x_i)]^2
Write the objective as S(\widehat{\beta}_0,\widehat{\beta}_1) = \sum_{i=1}^n [y_i-(\widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_1 x_i)]^2.
FOC

\def\sumn{\sum_{i=1}^{n}}
\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial S}{\partial \widehat{\beta}_0}=& -2 \sumn [y_i-(\widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_1 x_i)] = -2\sumn \widehat{u}_i = 0 \\\\
\frac{\partial S}{\partial \widehat{\beta}_1}=& -2 \sumn x_i\cdot [y_i-(\widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_1 x_i)] = -2\sumn x_i\cdot \widehat{u}_i = 0
\end{align*}

Dividing each by -2 leaves the two conditions OLS always satisfies:

\def\sumn{\sum_{i=1}^{n}}
\sumn \widehat{u}_i = 0 \;\;\;\text{and}\;\;\; \sumn x_i \widehat{u}_i = 0

OLS estimators: analytical formula

\def\sumn{\sum_{i=1}^{n}}
\begin{aligned}
  \widehat{\beta}_1 & = \frac{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})^2},\\\\
  \widehat{\beta}_0 & = \bar{y}-\widehat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}, \\\\
  \text{where} & \;\; \bar{y} = \sumn y_i/n \;\; \text{and} \;\;\bar{x} = \sumn x_i/n
\end{aligned}





Transcript

This is a small distinction with a large payoff later, so let’s be careful with it. An estimator is a rule, a formula that says what to do with whatever data you are handed. An estimate is the number that comes out when you feed that rule your particular data. The formula on screen is the estimator; six point five nine nine is the estimate, for these five hundred and forty-six houses. And here is why it matters. Hand the same estimator a different sample of houses and you get a different number out. The estimate moves around. That variability is the entire subject of the next lecture.

Estimators
Specific  rules (formula)  to use once you get the data

Estimates
Numbers you get once you plug values (your data) into the formula

In this lecture

the formula \widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum (x_i-\bar{x})^2} is the  estimator 
the number 6.599, which it returns for the HousePrices data, is the  estimate 

Feed the same estimator a different sample and you get a different estimate. That is the whole subject of the next lecture.

Transcript

Now that we have numbers we can write the estimated model out, and this is the object you would report in a paper. Price equals thirty-four thousand one hundred and thirty-six, plus six point five nine nine times lot size. It has a name worth knowing, the sample regression function, and it is our estimate of the population regression function, the expected value of price given lot size. Read the callout, because it holds the caveat students most often drop. Regression predicts an expected value, an average. It is not telling you what your house will sell for. It is telling you what houses like yours sell for on average.

Model to be estimated

price = \beta_0 + \beta_1 lotsize + u


Estimated Model
This is the estimated version of the expected value of y conditional on x.

price =  34136 + 6.599 \times lotsize

This is called  sample regression function (SRF) , and it is an estimation of E[price|lotsize], the  population regression function (PRF).



Important



OLS regression predicts the  expected  value of the dependent variable  conditional on the explanatory variables.
\widehat{\beta}_1 is an estimate of how a change in x affects the  expected  value of y.








Transcript

This is the fitted values idea from a moment ago, met again where you would actually reach for it. The fitted values element gives you the model’s prediction for each house in your data. That is useful when you want to compare predicted against actual: to plot one against the other, or to hunt down the houses your model gets most badly wrong. But notice the restriction. You can access the predicted values at the observed points by looking at the fitted.values element of the regression results.

title: 01-2: Univariate Regression: OLS Mechanics and Implementation
text:
R^2: Goodness of fit

What is it?Decompose yVisualizationR^2 componentsDefinition of R^2Caveat




Transcript

The last topic today is R-squared, and I want you to have the one-sentence version before any formulas arrive. R-squared measures how much better your model predicts the dependent variable than the laziest possible model does. And that lazy model is worth naming, because it is the benchmark the whole measure is built on: just guess the average price for every single house, ignoring lot size entirely. So R-squared answers one question. How much did knowing lot size actually buy me, over knowing nothing but the average? Everything in the next four tabs is machinery for turning that question into a number.

R^2 is a measure of how good your model is in predicting the dependent variable (explaining variations in the dependent variable)  compared  to just using the average of the dependent variable as the predictor.




Transcript

Before the formula, here is the decomposition it rests on, and it is only algebra. Any observed y-i splits into two pieces: the fitted value, y-hat-i, and the residual, u-hat-i. Now subtract the sample average, y-bar, from both sides, and read the three bullets. On the left, y-i minus y-bar, is how far this house’s price sits from the average price; that is the total deviation you are trying to account for. On the right, y-hat-i minus y-bar is the part your model explains, and u-hat-i is the part it does not. Every measure of fit compares those two right-hand pieces.

You can decompose observed value of y into two parts: fitted value and residual

y_i=\widehat{y}_i +\widehat{u}_i, \;\;\text{where}\;\; \widehat{y}_i = \widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_1 x_i

now, subtracting \bar{y} (sample average of y),

y_i-\bar{y}=\widehat{y}_i-\bar{y}+\widehat{u}_i


y_i-\bar{y}: how far away the actual value of y for ith observation from the sample average \bar{y} is (actual deviation from the mean)
\widehat{y_i}-\bar{y}: how far away the predicted value of y for ith observation from the sample average \bar{y} is (explained deviation from the mean)
\widehat{u_i}: the residual for ith observation





Transcript

Here is that split drawn for one real house, so the algebra has a picture attached to it. The red horizontal line is y-bar, the average price. The blue line is the fitted model. Now find the black dot over on the right: that is one house. The green arrow runs from the average up to the fitted line, and that is the explained part, what knowing this house’s lot size buys you. The purple arrow runs from the fitted line to where the house actually sold, and that is the residual, what the model missed. Green plus purple is the total deviation.

The three pieces, drawn for a  single  observation. The red line is \bar{y}; the blue line is the fitted model.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

green + purple together make up y_i-\bar{y}, the actual deviation from the mean
green alone, \widehat{y}_i-\bar{y}, is the part the model  explains 
purple alone, \widehat{u}_i, is the part it does  not 





Transcript

Three sums, and the names are more confusing than the mathematics, so take them slowly. Total sum of squares, SST, adds up the squared total deviations: how much price varies overall. Explained sum of squares, SSE, adds up the squared explained parts, the green arrows. Residual sum of squares, SSR, adds up the squared residuals, the purple arrows, and you have met this one already, because it is exactly the quantity OLS was chosen to minimize. One warning: some textbooks swap the letters SSE and SSR completely, so read the definition rather than trusting the acronym.

total sum of squares (SST)

SST\equiv \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\bar{y})^2

explained sum of squares (SSE) 
SSE\equiv \sum_{i=1}^{n}(\widehat{y}_i-\bar{y})^2

residual sum of squares (SSR) 
SSR\equiv \sum_{i=1}^{n}\widehat{u}_i^2





Transcript

Now the definition. R-squared is one minus SSR over SST. Where that comes from is the three lines below: total equals explained plus residual, rearrange, divide through by SST. So R-squared is equally the explained share, SSE over SST, and it sits between zero and one as long as your model includes an intercept. And here is the number for our regression, computed just below: about zero point two nine. Lot size accounts for roughly twenty-nine percent of the variation in house price. The other seventy-one percent is everything in u, bedrooms, location, condition, the year it sold.





Definition


R^2 = 1 - SSR/SST





Where did it come from?
\begin{align*}
& SST = SSE + SSR  \\
\Rightarrow & SSE = SST - SSR \\
\Rightarrow & SSE/SST = 1 - SSR/SST = R^2\\
\end{align*}
The value of R^2 always lies between 0 and 1 as long as an intercept is included in the econometric model.

What does it measure?
R^2 is a measure of how much improvement  in predicting the dependent variable  you’ve made by including independent variable(s) (y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x+u) compared to when simply using the mean of dependent variable as the predictor (y=\beta_0+u).

For our model


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

That is how much of the variation in house price lot size alone accounts for. The rest is everything in u — bedrooms, location, condition, the year it sold.




Transcript

Now the warning, and it is the most important thing on this slide. R-squared tells you nothing about whether you have estimated beta-one well. Read the two blocks. We can always check how well a model predicts the dependent variable, because we observe the dependent variable. We can never check how well we estimated beta-one, because nobody ever shows us the true beta-one. So we are in the awkward position of being able to measure the thing we do not much care about, and unable to measure the thing we do. That is exactly why the next topic is assumptions.

Important

R^2 tells  nothing  about how well you have estimated the causal ceteris paribus impact of x on y (\beta_1).
As economists, we typically do not care how well we can  predict  the dependent variable; we care how well we have  estimated  \beta_1. (We predict outcomes; we estimate parameters.)

Problem

While we observe the dependent variable (otherwise you cannot run regression), we cannot observe \beta_1.
So, we get to check how good estimated models are in predicting the dependent variable (which we do not care about), but we can  never  test whether they have estimated \beta_1 well.
This means that we need to carefully examine whether the  assumptions  necessary for good estimation of \beta_1 are satisfied (next topic).

title: 00: Introduction to Econometrics
text:
What econometrics is about

What?Steps in Econometric Analysis




Transcript

Let’s start with the simplest possible answer to the question, what is econometrics? We estimate quantitative relationships between variables. Notice the word quantitative. We are not satisfied with saying fertilizer helps yield; we want a number, in bushels per additional pound of nitrogen. Look at the three examples on the screen. Every one of them has the same shape: something you could change, and something you care about. Fertilizer and yield, campaign spending and votes, education and wages. That shape is going to follow you through the entire course. And notice that all three are questions somebody would pay money to have answered, which is really why this field exists at all.

What are we doing?
Estimate quantitative relationships between variables.

Examples

the impact of fertilizer on crop yield
the impact of political campaign expenditure on voting outcomes
the impact of education on wage





Transcript

Here is the whole workflow of an empirical project, start to finish. I want you to notice two things about this list. First, how much of it happens before any estimation: you formulate a question, you build an economic model of what is going on, you turn that into an econometric model, and only then do you collect data. Four steps of thinking before a single number gets computed. Second, notice that only the last two, the ones in blue, are what this course is about. That is not because the first four matter less. They matter enormously. It is that they are much harder to teach, and much easier to do badly.


formulation of the question of interest (what are you trying to find out?)
develop an economic model of the phenomenon you are interested in understanding (identify variables that matter)
turn the economic model into an econometric model
collect data
 estimate the model using econometrics 
 test hypotheses

title: 00: Introduction to Econometrics
text:
Go through the steps

Step 2: Economic ModelStep 3: Econometric modelStep 4: Collect dataSteps 5 and 6




Transcript

We will walk through those steps with one concrete example: does job training actually make workers more productive? Step two says write down an economic model, and here it is. Wage is some function f of education, experience, and training. That is all an economic model is at this stage, a claim about which things belong on the list. Notice what it does not say. It does not say how much each one matters, or even whether more education means a higher wage. It only names the variables you think are in play. And read the note at the bottom, because this list is deliberately short so we can follow it. A real paper’s model would be far more involved.

Example: Job training and worker productivity
wage = f(educ,exper,training)

wage: hourly wage
educ: years of formal education
exper: years of workforce experience
training: weeks spent in job training

Note
Depending on questions you would like to answer, the economic model can (and should) be much more involved




Transcript

Step three is where the model becomes something you can actually estimate, and it takes one big decision: you have to pick a form for that function f. Almost always we start by assuming it is linear, which gives you the equation on screen. Wage equals beta-zero, plus beta-one times education, plus beta-two times experience, plus beta-three times training, plus u. The betas are the parameters, and they are what you are after: each one answers how much wage moves when that variable moves. Now look hard at the u on the end. That is the error term, and it holds every other thing that affects a wage. Innate ability, luck, who your parents know. Remember it. It is where all our trouble comes from.

We have built a conceptual model:
wage = f(educ,exper,training)
Now, the form of the function f(\cdot) must be specified (almost always) before we can undertake an econometric analysis

wage = \beta_0 + \beta_1 educ + \beta_2 exper + \beta_3 training + u

\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3

are the  parameters  of the econometric model.
describe the directions and strengths of the relationship between wage and the factors used to determine wage in the model

u

is called error term
includes  ALL  the other factors that can affect wage other than the included variables (like innate ability)



We can collect data using various ways. Some of them include survey, websites, experiments. Let’s look at different data types:

Cross-sectional DataTime-series DataPanel (Longitudinal) Data




Transcript

Step four is data, and the kind of data you have decides which methods are even available to you, so it is worth naming the three types. This first one, cross-sectional, is a snapshot: many different units, people or farms or firms or counties, each observed once, at roughly one point in time. I say roughly because, as the second bullet points out, some of these families were surveyed in different weeks of the year. Look at the table below, which is real wage data in R. Each row is one worker; the columns are that worker’s wage, education, experience, and so on. There is no time dimension at all. Most of this course assumes data that looks exactly like this.


Sample of individuals, households, firms, cities, states, countries, or a variety of other units, taken at a given point in time
The data on all units do not correspond to precisely the same time period

some families surveyed during different weeks within a year

The second type is the mirror image: one unit, followed over time. The price of corn every month for thirty years, or the price of oil. Instead of many people once, it is one series many times. And I want to be upfront about the note in red. We are not going to teach time series methods in this course. That is not a slight on them. It is that observations sitting next to each other in time are related to each other in ways that break most of the assumptions we are about to make, and repairing that properly takes a course of its own. Panel data means you follow the same units over time: the same people surveyed every five years, the same sixty countries every year. Look at the table. The reason to care, and it will matter enormously in lecture ten, is that when you observe the same county twice, anything about that county that does not change can be differenced away, even if you never got to measure it.
